    Starting with OA Data

    Last updated on 2026-11-19 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do you organise data files within a project?
    • How do you load the packages and data needed for the dashboard?
    • How do you get a first overview of a dataset?
    • How do you filter a dataset down to a single institution?

    Objectives

    • Organise a data file within a project’s folder structure
    • Load the packages and data needed to work with the dataset
    • Get a first overview of a dataset’s size, columns and values
    • Filter a dataset to a single institution and add a column that records whether an article is open access

    The dataset

    Throughout the rest of this lesson, we work with a single CSV file, jct_oal_TA_dataset.csv. It contains data on articles that were published under transformative agreements, enriched with bibliographic metadata from OpenAlex. Each row is one article. Here is what each column means:

    column name description
    openalex_id article identifier given within the OpenAlex database
    doi digital object identifier of the article
    issn_l linking ISSN of the journal the article was published in
    ror Research Organization Registry (ROR) identifier of the corresponding author’s affiliated institution
    esac_id ESAC Registry identifier for the transformative agreement under which the article was published
    start_date transformative agreement term start date
    end_date transformative agreement term end date
    publication_date article publication date
    oa_status article open access status
    field primary subject field the article was assigned to, based on the classification of OpenAlex
    domain primary subject domain the article was assigned to, based on the classification of OpenAlex
    institution display name of the corresponding author’s affiliated institution
    publisher display name of the publisher the article was published by
    publication_year article publication year

    Organising your data

    Before loading data into our dashboard, create a data folder inside your project. You can do this by clicking the New Folder button in the Files pane (bottom right in RStudio), or by running this command once in the Console:

    R 

    dir.create("data")

    Then move jct_oal_TA_dataset.csv into that new folder, for example by dragging it there in your file manager.

    Loading packages and data

    We now work inside the dashboard document, in a chunk at the very top, above the first heading but below the YAML header. This chunk is for setup only, so it should not show anything on the dashboard. The chunk option to achieve this is #| include: false. Insert a new chunk (Ctrl+Alt+I / Cmd+Option+I) with the #| include: false option:

    R 

    #| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(DT)

oa_all <- read_csv("data/jct_oal_TA_dataset.csv")

    The code has two parts. First, the two library() lines load the packages we installed in the R episode: tidyverse gives us read_csv() for reading CSV files and the dplyr verbs from the previous episode, and DT is needed for creating an interactive table later. Second, read_csv() reads the dataset into the object oa_all.

    The path "data/jct_oal_TA_dataset.csv" is relative, this means RStudio looks for the data folder next to your .qmd file in the project directory. Run the chunk with the green play arrow so that the objects exist in your RStudio session.

    A first look at the data

    A full data exploration and cleaning step is its own topic and beyond the scope of this lesson. We will only get a general overview of the contents of the dataset and do minimal data preparation. We do not want the data preparation output displayed in our dashboard, so run the following lines in the RStudio Console, not in a code chunk of your dashboard.

    The dim() function tells you the dimensions of your data frame, that is how many rows and columns you are working with.

    R 

    dim(oa_all)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 231695     14

    The glimpse() function shows the number of rows, every column name, each columns data type and a preview of its first values, all in one compact view.

    R 

    glimpse(oa_all)

    OUTPUT 

    Rows: 231,695
Columns: 14

$ doi              <chr> "10.1145/3664595", "10.1145/3663666", "10.1021/acs.bi…
$ issn_l           <chr> "0360-0300", "1549-6325", "1525-7797", "1044-0305", "…
$ ror              <chr> "https://ror.org/01111rn36", "https://ror.org/01a77tt…
$ esac_id          <chr> "acm2022crui", "acm2023jisc", "acs2020crui", "acs2020…
$ start_date       <date> 2022-05-01, 2023-01-01, 2020-01-01, 2020-01-01, 2020…
$ end_date         <date> 2025-12-31, 2025-12-31, 2023-12-31, 2023-12-31, 2023…
$ publication_date <date> 2024-05-11, 2024-05-07, 2020-02-03, 2020-02-18, 2020…

    The count() function counts how often each value, or each combination of values, appears in the columns you provide. With the sort = TRUE argument the output is ordered by the most common values. We will provide the institution and the ror column names to the count() function. This gives us an overview of how many articles per institution are in our dataset.

    R 

    oa_all |>
  count(institution, ror, sort = TRUE)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 46 × 3

   <chr>                                       <chr>                     <int>

 3 Queen Mary University of London             https://ror.org/026zzn846  5895

# ℹ 36 more rows

    Filtering for a single institution

    The lesson dataset contains data for 46 institutions, but we want our dashboard to monitor open access for just one institution. We identify an institution by its ROR ID (Research Organization Registry identifier), which is unambiguous, unlike institution names that can be spelled in many ways. As an example we use the University of Göttingen.

    Back in the setup chunk of our dashboard, we store the ROR ID of the University of Göttingen in an object and filter the data based on it:

    R 

    #| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(DT)

oa_all <- read_csv("data/jct_oal_TA_dataset.csv")

my_ror <- "https://ror.org/01y9bpm73"

oa_df <- oa_all |>
  filter(ror == my_ror)

    Keeping the ROR in its own object my_ror at the top has the advantage that to build the dashboard for another institution, you change one line and render again.

    oa_df is the data frame the rest of lesson works with.

    Identifying open access articles

    For our OA monitoring dashboard, we want to know which articles are open access and which ones are closed. The column oa_status tells us how an article is available. We can use the count() function again to check which OA status values occur in the data:

    R 

    oa_df |>
  count(oa_status, sort = TRUE)

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 6 × 2
  oa_status     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 hybrid     3500
2 gold       1121
3 closed      728
4 green       374
5 bronze      231
6 diamond      38

    The column names the open access route (for example gold, hybrid or green) or says that an article is closed. But there is no column that directly answers the question: Is this article open access, yes or no? We will create such a column now.

    For this lesson an article is considered open access if its OA status is anything except “closed”. We record this in a new column is_oa, to which we assign the value TRUE for OA articles and the value FALSE for closed ones. To create the new column we add the mutate() function to our setup chunk:

    R 

    #| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(DT)

oa_all <- read_csv("data/jct_oal_TA_dataset.csv")

my_ror <- "https://ror.org/01y9bpm73"

oa_df <- oa_all |>
  filter(ror == my_ror) |>
  mutate(is_oa = oa_status != "closed")

    Saving a dataset

    We can save oa_df, now including the new column, as a CSV file, for example to share it with a colleague, or in case we do not want to load the bigger file every time our dashboard renders. This can be especially relevant if we work with a lot of data. We use the write_csv() function, which takes the data frame and a file path:

    R 

    write_csv(oa_df, file = "data/oa_df_goettingen.csv")

    After running this line in a code chunk or in the Console, a new file oa_df_goettingen.csv appears in the data folder of your project.

    Challenge

    Challenge: A list of gold OA articles

    A colleague from the library wants a list of all gold open access articles of your institution. She only needs three columns: doi, publisher and publication_year. Create this list from oa_df and save it as a CSV file in the data folder, so that you can send it to her.

    Use three steps one after another: filter() for the rows with oa_status equal to "gold", select() for the columns, and write_csv() to save the result.

    R 

    oa_gold <- oa_df |>
  filter(oa_status == "gold") |>
  select(doi, publisher, publication_year)

write_csv(oa_gold, file = "data/gold_articles_goettingen.csv")

    Remember to put "gold" in quotation marks and to use two equal signs (==) for comparing.

    Key Points

    • dim(), glimpse() and count() give a general overview of a new dataset
    • filter() narrows the data to the rows you need
    • mutate() adds or modifies a column
    • write_csv() saves a data frame as a CSV file
